opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes down to wanting to ask a clean scientific question rather than invent a new method. When I started looking at pruning, the field was full of papers proposing their own clever pruning techniques, each with its own hyperparameters, tricks, and evaluation setups. If I had come in with yet another bespoke method, any interesting result could have been dismissed as an artifact of my particular choices. People would ask whether it was the method doing the work or the phenomenon I was trying to study.

So I deliberately took the most standard, boring approach I could find: magnitude pruning, the kind of thing people had used for decades, going back to work like Han et al. You train the network, remove the weights with the smallest magnitudes, and look at what's left. It's simple, it's well understood, and everyone already accepts it as a reasonable baseline. If I could show something surprising using that, like the idea that these sparse subnetworks could be trained from the start if you reset them to their original initialization, then the finding said something about neural networks themselves rather than about my engineering.

There's also a humility piece. The people who came before had already figured out a lot about what works, and building on their foundation meant I didn't have to re-litigate all of that. I could focus my energy on the question I actually cared about: why can we prune so much after training, and what does that tell us about what's happening during training? Anchoring in prior work made the experiments more credible, easier to reproduce, and easier for others to build on.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Frankle chose standard magnitude pruning so the surprising result would speak to neural networks rather than his engineering or a newly invented method. This communicates keeping the paper focused on its findings rather than its algorithm.

r002.rationale: The candidate explains that a bespoke method could lead people to suspect the result was an artifact of his choices and to ask whether the method or the phenomenon produced it.

r003.rationale: The candidate says prior researchers had established what worked, and that building on their foundation made the experiments more credible and reproducible.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's mostly about discipline. Pruning is one of those areas where it's incredibly easy to fool yourself. There are a thousand knobs you could turn, and if I invent a brand-new pruning heuristic and then make a claim about, say, the lottery ticket hypothesis, nobody can tell whether the interesting result comes from the phenomenon I'm trying to study or from some quirk of the method I just made up.

So when we were doing the lottery ticket work, we deliberately used the simplest, most boring thing we could: iterative magnitude pruning, which goes back to Han, Pool, Tran, and Dally, and really all the way to LeCun's Optimal Brain Damage in the late eighties. The point wasn't to beat the state of the art on sparsity. The point was to ask a scientific question about training, and for that you want the pruning procedure to be a known quantity. If the method is already well understood and well characterized by other people, then it's a fixed reference point, and whatever I observe on top of it is more likely to be real.

There's also a reproducibility angle. If I anchor in something standard, other people can rerun the experiment without having to reverse-engineer my design choices, and they can tell me quickly if I've made a mistake. That happened to us, and it made the work better. The other thing I'd say is that this field has a bit of a tendency to publish a new heuristic every few months, each with slightly different experimental setups, and it's genuinely hard to know what's a real improvement. Starting from established baselines is a small way of pushing back on that. You contribute the one new idea you actually want to test, and you hold everything else constant.

r001.rationale: Frankle says they chose the simplest, established pruning method so the paper could study a scientific question about training rather than optimize the pruning algorithm.

r002.rationale: The response says an invented heuristic could make it unclear whether results came from the phenomenon or a method quirk, but does not explain that departures may invite suspicion they were needed to obtain the reported results.

r003.rationale: It cites established prior methods as known, well-characterized reference points that make the design choices defensible and reproducible.

astra-6.text:
Because I want to isolate what’s actually new in the experiment. Pruning already has a substantial history, so if there’s an established approach we can use, that gives us a useful starting point. If I introduce a new pruning method at the same time that I’m asking a new question about the network, it becomes hard to tell which change explains the result.

So I’d rather start with something simple and familiar, like pruning weights based on their magnitude, and ask what we can learn from that. It makes the comparison clearer, and it means the argument doesn’t depend on convincing you that my particular pruning algorithm is better.

r001.rationale: The response favors a simple, familiar pruning method so the experiment can focus on what is new and its results, rather than on proving the pruning algorithm is better.

r002.rationale: It says changing the pruning method alongside the research question would make results harder to interpret, but does not say such departures could invite suspicion that they were necessary to obtain the results.

r003.rationale: It cites pruning’s substantial history and established approaches as a useful basis for choosing a familiar method.

sol-6.1.text: I think it’s important to build on what people have already figured out. Pruning has a long history, and if I introduce a new pruning method at the same time that I’m trying to study something about neural networks, it becomes hard to tell where the results are coming from. Are they telling us something fundamental about the network, or something particular about my method? Starting with an established approach gives us a baseline and lets us isolate the question we actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response says using an established pruning approach keeps the study focused on the question about the network and helps separate those results from effects of a new method.

r002.rationale: It says a new method would make results harder to interpret, but does not say departures from prior choices could raise suspicion that they were needed to obtain the results.

r003.rationale: The response treats established prior work as a reason to build on and use an existing approach as the study’s baseline.
